properties.description:
Every claim records a seat — machine:pid:mint, minted once per session with zero coordination — defaulting to the session making it, overridable with a durable handle (a fleet worker name). claim_report then COMPUTES liveness rather than storing it: nothing writes 'I am alive', so nothing can be stale. A claim whose session is no longer attached is reported `gone`, listed in `stale` with its note intact, and EXCLUDED from overlaps, because a collision with nobody is not a collision and reporting it as one is how an advisory report starts lying. A claim from another machine, or from before seats were recorded, is `unknown` and still counts as a possible collision — reading it as free would invite somebody to take work that is actively being done.

HOW LIVENESS IS COMPUTED DEPENDS ON WHO MINTED THE SEAT, and this is the part that was wrong until 2026-08-08. A seat carrying ANOTHER process's pid is answered by asking the operating system whether that process still exists — so a seat left behind by a previous shared server correctly reads `gone` after a `--stop-shared` bounce. A seat THIS process minted cannot be answered that way, because under `--shared` every seat is minted by the daemon and the daemon's pid is alive by definition: the probe asked 'is the server running?', to which the answer is always yes, and `gone` was unreachable. Measured in dev_storyflow (w-613d836b, 2026-08-07): a worker that had died hours earlier still read as holding its region, and this capability was status `verified` throughout. Those seats are now answered from the sessions the server is actually holding — a lease registered on attach and released by Drop, so a client that crashes retires its seat exactly like one that exits cleanly. The registry answers only for seats the process itself issued; anything else falls through to the probe, so a bare mint_seat elsewhere in the process cannot make an unrelated seat read as a ghost.

WHY THE ORIGINAL CHECK DID NOT CATCH IT, recorded because the shape recurs: the property was true under the stdio transport, where the serving process WAS the session. `--shared` became the installed default, the world moved, and nothing recomputes a check when the deployment model changes underneath it. The test that covered it still passed, because in a test process the server and the session are the same thing.
properties.name: A claim names the session that made it, and a claim nobody is working says so
